result: Predictability of movement cues affected reaction times but not movement speed. Reaction times were significantly shorter in the predictable condition for both start and stop cues (C38, C39), with a main effect of condition (C36) and a condition*movement type interaction (C37). However, angular speed changes were similar across conditions when aligned to action onset (C34), indicating that movements were initiated earlier in the predictable condition but executed at the same speed (C40).
evaluation: The behavioral findings are well-supported by appropriate statistical tests (rmANCOVA with significant main effects and interactions, post-hoc t-tests with effect sizes). The data clearly demonstrate that predictability affects timing of movement initiation but not execution speed, with convergent evidence from both movement-aligned and cue-aligned analyses (C34, C35).

result: Movement initiation and termination are associated with characteristic beta oscillation patterns in STN and motor cortex. Starting to turn the wheel produced prominent bilateral beta suppression in both STN and M1 (C41-C44), while stopping resulted in a beta rebound in the same regions (C45-C48). The beta suppression was bilateral while the beta rebound was more lateralized to the contralateral hemisphere (C49).
evaluation: These findings are strongly supported by cluster-based permutation tests with highly significant p-values (all p≤0.003) and are consistent with established literature on movement-related beta dynamics. The lateralization analysis provides additional statistical support (C49). The results replicate well-known phenomena in motor control, lending credibility to the experimental approach.

result: Movement reversals show distinct beta oscillation patterns compared to complete stops. No clear beta rebound was observed during reversals (C5, C55), with high inter-patient variability in STN responses (C56). When increases occurred, they differed spectrally from stop-related rebounds, often lacking the low-beta component (C57, C102). Instead, cortex showed transient beta suppression related to re-acceleration (C100), while some patients showed high-beta increases in STN compatible with brief pause processing (C101).
evaluation: The distinction between brief pauses and complete stops is well-documented through multiple lines of evidence: absence of significant group-level effects (C55), individual patient variability (C56), spectral differences (C57, C102), and differential cortical vs. subcortical responses (C100, C101). The interpretation is strengthened by citations to prior work on low/high-beta dissociation (C103).

result: Reversals involve bilateral cortical beta suppression with ipsilateral predominance due to floor effects. Reversals were associated with alpha/beta suppression in M1, stronger ipsilaterally (C59, C61, C62), occurring after the turning point (C60). This pattern reflects a floor effect: contralateral beta was already maximally suppressed during ongoing movement (C65, C92), while ipsilateral beta was at intermediate levels allowing further suppression (C64, C91). Bilateral beta modulation was selective to acceleration phases (C93, C94).
evaluation: The floor effect explanation is well-supported by converging evidence from baseline-corrected analyses (C59-C62), whole-recording baseline analyses (C63-C65), and statistical tests showing significant ROI*movement interactions (C61). The interpretation that ipsilateral M1 recruitment is selective to acceleration (C94) is a reasonable inference from the data pattern, though causality cannot be established.

result: Unpredictable movement cues enhance STN-cortex beta coherence modulations. Event-related increases in STN-cortex beta coherence were stronger in the unpredictable condition (C10, C172), most pronounced in MSMC (C173), and primarily driven by increased coherence following stops (C174, C175). This effect was not due to baseline shifts (C176, C177) but reflected intensified event-related interactions (C178). Beta power suppression at movement start was reduced in the unpredictable condition (C67).
evaluation: The predictability effects are supported by appropriate statistical tests (main effect: F(1,15)=8.684, p=0.010; C172) and control analyses ruling out baseline confounds (C176). The interpretation that unpredictability enhances STN-cortex interactions (C178, C79) is reasonable given the data, though the mechanistic link to 'caution' remains speculative. The convergent effects on coherence and power strengthen the overall conclusion.

result: STN-cortex coherence shows movement-related modulations similar to power, with cortical drive of STN in the beta band. STN-cortex coherence exhibited beta suppression at movement start and beta rebound at stop, plus gamma increases at start (C69). Unlike cortical power, coherence did not decrease during reversal re-acceleration and even increased qualitatively (C70, C71). Granger causality analysis revealed significant cortical drive of STN beta activity from both M1 and MSMC, bilaterally (C166-C170).
evaluation: The coherence findings are supported by cluster-based permutation tests with significant p-values (C69). The Granger causality analysis appropriately uses time-reversed controls and shows consistent directional effects across hemispheres and cortical regions (C167-C170), with significant main effect (F(7,9)=3.443, p=0.044; C166). The qualitative observation about reversal-related coherence increases (C71) is appropriately cautious but could benefit from statistical testing.

result: Gamma oscillations show modest movement-related changes that are not modulated by predictability. Gamma power increased at movement start in contralateral STN (C51) and decreased at stop in contralateral STN and M1 (C52, C53), but these changes were much smaller than beta modulations (C54). Gamma power and coherence were not affected by predictability (C68, C179), and no directional drive was detected in the gamma band (C171).
evaluation: The gamma findings are adequately supported by statistical tests showing significant effects where claimed (C51-C53) and non-significant effects for predictability (C68, C171, C179). The characterization of gamma changes as 'much smaller' than beta (C54) is a qualitative observation that appears justified from the figures. However, the functional interpretation of gamma changes is appropriately limited given the lack of consensus in the field (C115).

result: The beta rebound occurs after movement has already slowed and likely serves a post-movement feedback function rather than causing stopping. The beta rebound occurred only at the end of movement sequences when stopping was already underway (C110), making a causal role in stopping implausible (C111). Instead, it likely serves as post-movement feedback for motor plan confirmation/updating (C112) or motor program clearance (C113).
evaluation: The timing argument against a causal role is well-supported by the data showing beta rebound occurs after movement has slowed (C110). The alternative interpretations (C112, C113) are appropriately presented as speculative ('likely,' 'might') and supported by citations to prior work. This represents a reasonable inference from the temporal data, though the specific functional role remains uncertain.

result: The low-beta component of the beta rebound must be avoided during movement changes to prevent slowing re-acceleration. Based on prior findings that beta rebound slows reaction times (C104), reduces corticospinal excitability (C105), and that beta must decrease for movement initiation (C106), the authors conclude that the low-beta rebound needs to be avoided during ongoing action changes (C107).
evaluation: This conclusion (C107) is an inference based on cited prior work (C104-C106) rather than direct evidence from the current study. While the logic is reasonable, the claim about 'needing to be avoided' implies a functional necessity that is not directly tested. The current study shows absence of low-beta rebound during reversals but does not establish whether this absence is functionally necessary or merely correlative.

result: Reduced beta suppression in the unpredictable condition reflects lower motor preparation. Beta suppression at movement start was weaker in the unpredictable condition (C86), consistent with prior MEG and EEG studies showing reduced beta suppression with uncertainty (C87, C88). However, no effect of predictability on beta rebound was found (C90).
evaluation: The finding of reduced beta suppression is supported by statistical tests (C67: interaction F(2,14)=4.206, p=0.037) and aligns with prior literature (C87, C88). The interpretation as 'lower motor preparation' (C86) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The absence of predictability effects on beta rebound (C90) is clearly stated and appropriately contrasted with prior work (C89).

result: This study provides first evidence for decreased STN gamma power when stopping continuous movement in response to visual cues. The authors report a decrease in STN gamma power at stop (C52), which they claim is the first evidence for this pattern with visual cues and continuous movement (C119), though they acknowledge that different methodological choices might yield different results (C120). Prior studies with auditory cues showed increases (C116, C117) or decreases (C118) depending on study design.
evaluation: The novelty claim (C119) is difficult to evaluate without comprehensive literature review. The authors appropriately acknowledge methodological factors that could affect results (C120) and note the lack of consensus in the field (C115). However, the claim of 'first evidence' is weakened by the acknowledgment that the result might be methodology-dependent and the small effect size of gamma changes (C54).

result: The study's findings are likely generalizable beyond the PD patient population despite limitations. While acknowledging sample size limitations (C121, C122) and age confounds (C123, C124), the authors argue their findings approximate healthy brain function because patients were on medication (C125, C126), findings match those in other populations (C127), and results align with cognitive theories (C128).
evaluation: The generalizability argument is reasonable but not definitive. The medication normalization claim (C126) is supported by citations, but 'normalization' does not mean complete restoration to healthy function. The convergence with other populations (C127) is encouraging but limited to specific findings (start/stop dynamics). The sample size (n=20) is appropriate for this type of study (C122) but still limits statistical power for detecting subtle effects or individual differences.

result: High inter-patient variability in STN reversal responses may reflect recording site differences or overlapping stop/go processes. The study cannot provide a general description of STN reversal responses due to patient variability (C132), possibly due to recording site variation (C133) or temporal overlap of stop and go processes (C134) that may not be resolvable with macro-electrode recordings (C135).
evaluation: The acknowledgment of variability (C132) is honest and supported by the data (C56). The proposed explanations (C133-C135) are appropriately speculative and supported by citations to prior work. This represents appropriate scientific caution about the limitations of the findings rather than overinterpreting variable data.

result: Movement context affects beta oscillations in basal ganglia-cortex loops, with unpredictable scenarios involving enhanced beta synchronization. The study demonstrates that brief pauses and complete stops have distinct oscillatory profiles (C136), and that unpredictable movement scenarios involve enhanced subthalamo-cortical beta synchronization (C137, C11), highlighting the role of long-range beta coherence in coordinating unpredictable movements (C138). Beta oscillations better reflect sequence boundaries than within-sequence changes (C12).
evaluation: These summary conclusions are well-supported by the multiple specific findings throughout the paper. The distinction between brief pauses and stops is documented in C5, C55-C58, C100-C103. The predictability effects are supported by C10, C67, C172-C178. The claim about sequence boundaries vs. within-sequence changes (C12) is supported by the strong start/stop effects vs. weak/variable reversal effects. These represent appropriate high-level synthesis of the detailed findings.
